utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Do you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, we will briefly go over one subject and then I will complete my examination-in-chief. Yesterday we broke off on this subject, and you said that it was from about September/October 1992 you worked on the work of recruitment and sending to the army. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that's where we broke off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like you to explain, if you can explain something, so that we can understand one thing. Can you tell us: What recruitment? Can you tell us: What did you do and what was the procedure involved?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law on the army, when young men are 17, they enter into the military register. When they reach the age of 18, they then go through a procedure of medical check-ups in order to assess their ability to serve in the army. This is what we call recruitment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So this is just checking the ability to serve in the army; is that correct, the definition I've just given you, and of course entering into the military register?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. However, after the recruitment is over, when the recruit is 18, and provided that he has completed his secondary school, he then goes to serve a military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So if I've understood you correctly, a person who has reached the age of 18, after they finish the secondary school, that's when they can be sent to serve the military service?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. That's what the law provided for. Now, the age has been moved to 19, but at that time, the law changed in 1996, but at that time it was the age of 18, provided that the person has completed secondary education.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, before you came here to testify, the Defence of Mr. Zaric asked you to check through the registers of the municipality of Bosanski Samac data regarding the recruitment and sending to the -- serve in the military service of Mirel Zaric, son of Mr. Simo Zaric. Can you tell us: When was he recruited and when was he sent to serve the military service? Did he serve, et cetera? How is this visible in your military register at the Ministry of Defence in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our register at the Ministry of Defence, Mirel Zaric was born in 1974. He was entered into the military register in 1991, in February. He was recruited in 1992, in February, i.e., a medical check-up was carried out and it was established that he was able to serve the military service, and that was in February 1992. In the school year of 1992/1993, Mirel was in the fourth year of the secondary school of economy. Following the completion of that school in 1993, he was sent to do his military service in August 1993. He spent one year in the army, until August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So there was nothing unusual or any situations that were not in accordance with the then regulations to do with him serving the military service?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the provisions of the law, there were no problems at all. Everything was in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And according to your knowledge and register, he served his military service for one year, according to the law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law provided for an eight-month military service, but there was a provision saying that everybody had to serve a year, and he served for a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In December 1992, was it possible to consider, according to the regulations that were valid then, could anyone have thought that Mirel Zaric was a deserter from the army and that he did not respond to the call for recruitment?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that Zaric sent to this organ of the National Defence, that he sent a certificate that he was a full-time student of the secondary school, he acted in accordance with the law, and it could not have been considered that he was a deserter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Any other counsel who wish to ask questions? Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic. In the name of the defence of Mr. Miroslav Tadic, I will ask you a few questions. Sir, Mr. Simic, when you are answering questions of my colleague Mr. Lazarevic, you described your duty shifts at the embankment, and also your military engagement, if we can call it that. Could you tell me: In these first few days after the 16th, 17th of April, did you notice that some people around you were wearing white armbands, whether they were either civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did notice. In fact, myself, I received a white armband, which I put above the elbow of my left arm, just like all the civilians that were on duty on this defence embankment, and I saw that the soldiers also had an armband on their left shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain for the record on which arm was that armband? What was its size? And can you show on which part of your arm?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was above the left elbow. I don't remember the size. This was just a white armband.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, the witness indicated the part of -- above his left elbow as being the place where he wore his white armband.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Simic, can you tell me: These soldiers that were also on duty with you, how did they wear this white armband? Where was it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the shoulder. It was over the part of -- the part of the uniform that is on top of the shoulder. I'm not sure, because I didn't serve in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like the record to indicate that the witness indicated his left shoulder, as this is where the soldiers that were on duty with him, that's where they wore the white armband.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you were asked by Mr. Lazarevic and you answered that sometime after the 12th of May, 1992, you came to work at the communications centre, at the secretariat for National Defence. You also described how you activated the equipment through the ACU batteries. Could you tell us: Before you came to that centre to work, do you have any knowledge that this centre had worked before the electricity was cut off, that is, before you became involved in it and before it started to operate?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was talking to my colleague Milos Micic, who was the first one who came to the secretariat to work, sometime after a couple of days, two or three days after the 17th of April, and he told me, considering that he was frequently on the premises of the centre for reporting and he knew how to handle this equipment, so he told me that he would switch on the radio equipment. His desire was to hear what was happening in the neighbouring municipalities, because he was able to follow the conversation of the colleagues -- from the colleagues from other centres. So he did make some notes in that notebook which was used as of November 1991. And he used this radio equipment while there was electricity, for a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you just opened up a subject. Can you tell me about this notebook, the notebook that you just mentioned? And you described before this Trial Chamber yesterday how you kept it. Was this the communication centre's notebook that had been kept before, or did you just continue to put in your observations?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the notebook where data was entered, as of November 1991, until the 16th of April, and it was done practically on a daily basis. This was kept on the desk. So the colleague, during that period, when he was there by himself, he was also using it, entering his observations. And then I continued to write in this notebook. So there is other data in it, not just about the negotiations between the representatives from Odzak and Samac. This notebook was not just for the negotiations, notes between Samac and Odzak. I really kept entering data for me and for the work that I was doing. I was keeping notes, because later on we had checks by the people -- by the officials from the Ministry of Defence. So this was a notebook was a proof for me that I was working on something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So this was proof that you used the equipment for official purposes, for the needs of the organs that you worked for?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: What did you all enter? What is it that you entered into that notebook? Was it about the shelling, information requests? Can you just describe that to us in a few lines.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that notebook you have data about the shelling of the town, on several occasions, about the casualties caused by the shelling, about the shelling of the town by an agricultural plane from Croatia, then there were those other information that we received from citizens and also their requests for assistance, if we could establish contact with their relatives in other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, can you tell me: This radio link, was it on all the time?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The radio connection was not on all the time, because there was no source of electricity. As I said, I used ACU batteries, and so I had to save them, because occasionally I had to recharge them. Later on I managed to find a small generator, but then there was a problem with fuel. So the radio equipment was occasionally off; in fact, it was more off than on. It operated according to the needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, can you tell me: Was that why you also put in the subjects and the notes to be discussed at certain meetings, apart from negotiations between Odzak and Samac?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, that was one of the reasons. This was saving the energy, so that I would be able to give the necessary assistance when conversations were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My name is Phillip Weiner. I'm with the Office of the Prosecutor and I'm going to ask you some questions this morning. You were just talking about the radio link and how you were one of nine municipalities in that radio link region; isn't that correct? Isn't that correct, sir? You were one of nine municipalities which were part of this radio link: Doboj, Samac, and several of the municipalities. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you talked about how you activated the radio system. Now, during this time, while you were using the radio system, were you ever able to learn from Doboj or elsewhere what was happening in these other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard from Doboj that they were in negotiations with Bosanski Brod in relation to some exchanges. But as far as the situation in Doboj was concerned, I was not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what about the other municipalities? Did you ever hear them on the radio discussing any of their situations? Because your predecessor put notes about some of the other communities what was happening, as you just testified this morning. Did you overhear conversations about what was happening with other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard frequently that a colleague from Bosanski Brod informed the colleague in Tesanj and in Maglaj about an airplane going in their direction. I presume that the colleague in Bosanski Brod was in connection, probably with some centre for observation, so he was forwarding information to the colleagues in Tesanj and Maglaj about the movement of JNA planes. And then on the basis of that, they would then alarm the towns, according to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, the municipality of Teslic was part of that regional radio system, was it not?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that municipality of Teslic is located right next to Doboj, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the president of the Crisis Staff was a Nikola Perisic, who was kind of a well-known figure in Bosnia-Herzegovina; were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first time I hear that name. I don't know that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, were you also aware, or did you learn through the radio system or through the press that in the late spring and summer, Serbian paramilitaries and the police forces had taken over the town of Teslic? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, and such pieces of information probably would not have been forwarded through this radio link. That could also be followed not just by the colleagues of Serb ethnicity, but also by persons of other ethnicities. We did not forward such data to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, did you learn about this: That after this take over, or at some point in late May and June, paramilitaries from the group known as the Red Berets, one of the most violent paramilitary groups, if not the most violent in Bosnia, unlawfully arrested non-Serb civilians, beat and tortured them, robbed them, raped them, murdered them? Were you aware of that, sir? The same things that were happening in Samac. Were you aware of that happening in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with the question, but I believe that there are two questions in one. First, my colleague was referring to Teslic. And frankly, I don't see the relevance of the situation in Teslic in this case. And then the other part of the question, just as it was in Bosanski Samac. So I believe that this one should be divided in two questions and put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it with the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Serbian paramilitaries known as the Red Berets, one of the most violent of all the paramilitary groups in Bosnia, unlawfully arrested non-Serb civilians, beat and tortured them, robbed them, raped them, and murdered them? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, were you aware that the Serbian Crisis Staff president was appalled by this conduct and had a strike force come to Teslic and arrested all of the paramilitaries? Were you aware of that? Were you aware of the manner that they resolved this problem in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object. The indictment covers the area of the municipality of Samac and municipality of Odzak. As far as what was happening in Teslic is concerned, that is totally irrelevant to this case and has no bearing regarding the trial in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's highly relevant. We've heard testimony in this case that -- we've heard different types of testimony. One, that the Crisis Staff was frightened of these paramilitaries, that there was nothing that they could do about the paramilitaries. One of the defendants testified that there was nothing that they could do about the paramilitaries, and one or more of his witnesses testified to the same. However, in a neighbouring municipality, or a municipality a distance away, which was part of this same radio group, which also was a fellow member in the SAO, or Serbian Autonomous region of Bosnia, this president of the Crisis Staff in Teslic was a vice-president of the Serbian Autonomous region, as was Blagoje Simic, a defendant in this case. When they saw what happened, they were appalled, they were scared, but they acted. And you can look at that situation as opposed to what happened in Samac, where they sat on their hands and did nothing. That's why we believe it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I haven't given you leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is sustained because we do not know the terms of reference of the Crisis Staff in Teslic. We also do not have evidence as to what type of paramilitaries and what their mission was in Teslic. And in any case, Teslic is not part of the indictment. So the objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And sorry, Your Honour, may I have a word?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: About what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: About -- just for the record, because my learned friend just mentioned that my client was a vice-president of the SAO of northern Bosnia, which is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In which line?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's line -- it's page 11, line 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, my client was a deputy, was a member of the Assembly of the SAO northern Bosnia. So maybe it's a kind of mistake in the translation. In the indictment, there is a word "deputy," which is assemblyman or a member, not deputy vice-president and not vice-president. Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, there is an exhibit which indicates he is a vice-president. He has denied being a vice-president. However, there is an exhibit before the court that says he was elected a vice-president.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, this is an issue at the dispute, and also according to the Rule 92 bis witnesses and some other exhibit, we shall clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. This is a matter which will be decided upon after all the evidence is on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified about what happened on April 17th, how you were woken up by the shooting. Do you recall that, testifying yesterday about that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware over the next few days that a Serbian municipality of Samac had been established?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you learn that a Crisis Staff was formed and Blagoje Simic, the defendant -- one of the defendants in this case, had been elected or named its president? Had you learned about that over the next few days?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that when I started working for the secretary for National Defence, that is, in the intelligence and information centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And had you learned that on the 17th and 18th, that Serbian forces, including volunteers from Serbia and Serbian police, were in the act of controlling or taking over all the vital buildings and facilities in the town of Samac? Did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you aware, sir, that the elected government was no longer in power, that a Serbian Crisis Staff was in power instead?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know who was running the municipality, whether there was a government or a different body that had taken over the functions of the government. I was not really involved in politics. I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, sir, you've testified on the following day, on the 17th -- or later that day on the 17th, you attended a meeting at a neighbour's home, a 4th Detachment meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I must object. This is really not what the witness said, that it was a meeting of the 4th Detachment. He said that he was called to come to the house of one of his neighbours. And then that later some members of the detachment came. That was not the meeting of the members of the 4th Detachment. I mean, I have a problem just the way the question is put.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd be happy to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You attended a meeting at a neighbour's house where members of the 4th Detachment were present; isn't that correct, sir? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not in the house, it was outside the house. We gathered and we were told that we were to stand guard next to the defensive embankment, and we were all handed out tasks as to where we would be on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it was someone from the 4th Detachment that was giving out orders?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably from the 4th Detachment. He was wearing a JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were ordered to guard one of the river banks; isn't that correct, the soldiers who were there were ordered to guard one of the river banks, take up defensive positions?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Which meant that you were there to protect the town from an attack by taking up defensive positions. You were there to prevent an outside attack, or an attack from the outside.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a position to prevent anything. I was not armed. I was merely observing from my house, which is part of that neighbourhood, and I believed that it was my duty to place myself at their disposal and to participate in securing the embankment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The soldiers, by securing the embankment, were preventing from an attack -- protecting the town from an attack from the other side of the embankment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the army's role was. There must have been a role for the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, if they're in a defensive position, then they're preparing to defend against an assault; isn't that correct, or a potential assault?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably they were preparing to defend against a potential assault.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you assisted them by observing, by watching, and you were watching for anyone who would come across and attack, or any troop movements moving towards the embankment that you were protecting, meaning that the soldiers were protecting?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was merely observing, to see if there was any movement or if anyone was moving towards the embankment, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Correct. You were watching to see if any troops or soldiers or paramilitaries or any groups from outside the town moved towards the embankment, where the soldiers from the JNA or the 4th Detachment were in a defensive position; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across the River Bosna, there is the Croatian village of Prud, and the expectation was that army troops of the HVO or of the Croatian regular army would be stationed there and that they might attack the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you were watching from your position inside of a house to see if troops -- if there was any troop movements, while the other soldiers that were from the 4th Detachment or the JNA were in the defensive embankments also watching towards the Prud area?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you didn't receive any orders to retake the town --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have a problem with this question. Is my colleague referring to this witness particularly? Did he get orders or --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you received your orders to establish defensive positions, there was no order given by the JNA soldier that: I want you to go in and retake the town. That order was not given to you, to those JNA troops. You weren't present for any of those types of orders, were you?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not receive any such order. As a civilian, I probably could not have retaken the town. I don't have the military expertise needed for that, so probably I would not have been part of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, sir. My question to you is: While you were receiving the orders, listening, as everyone was receiving the orders, no order was given to retake the town. You weren't present for that order; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not present, nor did I know of any such orders being given.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you never heard any order being given to remove the Serbian volunteers and the Serbian police that have invaded the town of Bosanski Samac. You didn't hear that order either, because it wasn't given. You don't recall ever hearing that order; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who took the Serbian town of Samac. I don't know about any paramilitaries. I was in that district, as simple as that, and I didn't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question is, listen carefully: You weren't present -- you did not hear any order, just whether or not you heard any order that you were to remove the Serbian volunteers and the Serbian police that have taken the town. You didn't hear that order given; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that order being given, nor did I know who had taken the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you didn't hear an order being given on that date you were to remove the Serbian Crisis Staff, go into -- the troops are to go into town and remove the Serbian Crisis Staff. You didn't hear that order either.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard about the Crisis Staff, as I said, when I came to work the first day. But prior to that, I hadn't even been aware of the existence of the Crisis Staff, so I never heard of any such order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Finally, sir: You didn't hear any order, while those orders were given by that JNA soldier, that you are to reinstate the elected government of Bosanski Samac, you're to go into town and reinstate the elected government of Bosanski Samac. You didn't hear that order being given either, did you?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had our own duty roster, and I came whenever it was my turn to come. But there weren't any meetings, nor did I ever hear anything related to the question you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the office -- the soldiers of the 4th Detachment followed their orders and they did set up defensive positions on the river bank; isn't that correct, sir, as they were told?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object only for one fact. How could this witness possibly know? He wasn't a member of the 4th Detachment. We already heard that. How could he comment on having any knowledge about orders given to the soldiers of the 4th Detachment? My colleague should first establish the basis for this question. Is there any base for this question to be posed to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has testified he went to his neighbour's house. There were soldiers from the 4th Detachment there. A JNA officer, a JNA soldier came and gave them orders to set up a defensive position. He was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He's testified it's a hundred metres from his home, and he's helping them, so he should be able to answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, he will answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the soldiers at your neighbour's home that were given those orders by the JNA officer to set up defensive positions on the river bank, they did it, defensive positions were set up on the river bank facing Prud; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defensive embankment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you assisted them by sitting in a house each day and observing or doing -- performing surveillance, looking towards the area of Prud, watching for military troops that would be coming?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I've said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, were you aware that the JNA had sent some vehicles, either armoured vehicles or tanks, to assist the soldiers? Did you see any of those tanks or armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I neither knew about those, nor did I see them. My house is just next to the embankment [as interpreted], and across the embankment there is nothing. There are fields, agricultural land.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one small correction for the transcript. On page 19, line 22, I think -- yes. "My house is just next to the embankment." He wasn't talking about his house, but the house where he was on his duty. So maybe just this "my house" was not correct. Maybe "the house where I was."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner can ask the witness to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the house that you were doing the observations from, was that next to the embankment?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the distance between the embankment and the house was perhaps five or six metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And your personal house -- I'm sorry. That was not your personal house?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That wasn't my house. My house is a hundred metres further off from the embankment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you aware that soldiers or members of the 4th Detachment were collecting weapons? Were you aware of that, while they were also watching the embankment? Collecting weapons from civilians.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So the only thing you were aware of is what you were doing on your street for approximately -- for approximately three weeks?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only that. Only what we were doing in relation to the defensive embankment, observing it merely, and nothing else. I was a civilian. I did not attend any military meetings, so I didn't have any information related to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And not only were you not a member of the military, although you were helping them, you weren't politically active, you weren't a member of any political party; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, as I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's move to May -- to the situation that you described in May at the radio room. You were present on two occasions when Simo Zaric spoke with officials from Odzak; isn't that correct? You testified about portions of those conversations yesterday.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you recall during the first conversation Simo Zaric saying to the people in Odzak that he would consult with members from the Crisis Staff about the Odzak proposals relating to any exchange of civilians? Do you recall that conversation, or something to that extent?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that part of the conversation. I was in and out of the room, as I told you. So all -- I've told you all I can remember, after all this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I realise you didn't take any notes in the conversation and you weren't in there for the entire conversation, but Simo Zaric, sir, has given a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, and on April 2nd he gave one of three statements, and he stated that he told the Odzak officials that he would convey their proposals to the Crisis Staff. Does that -- and he said that at page 79 in 141 ter. Does that refresh your recollection at all? Do you recall that at all, any conversation him telling them whatever proposals you make concerning exchanges, I will relay those, or I will convey these proposals to the members of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac? Does that refresh your recollection, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that does not refresh my recollection. I simply can't confirm that it was the way he had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you have any reason to doubt what Simo Zaric told the Prosecutor's office? Do you have any reason to believe that it's not true, that statement that he gave that he would convey their proposals to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what Simo said. I can neither confirm nor deny. I know that I personally didn't hear about this, but I would not like to say anything further about his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. My question to you is: Are you aware of any bias or prejudice which would cause Simo to lie about that specific statement? That's my question to you.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, Simo Zaric further told the Prosecutor's office during that conversation that he did in fact advise the Crisis Staff president, Stevan Todorovic, and some Crisis Staff members concerning those Odzak proposals for an exchange, which came out of that first radio conversation. Do you recall him saying that to you? Did he ever tell you that after the -- did he ever tell you that at that second radio conversation, that he had advised the Crisis Staff about what was going on with relation to Odzak's proposals for exchange, or were you present when he could have told any of the others in the room that information?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, excuse me. I think it would only be fair to read out what exactly Simo Zaric has said, because the interview that Simo Zaric gave and what my learned friend and colleague Weiner said later, the two are not identical. I think we would probably do well to read the very sentence that Simo Zaric stated, since we're asking for his commentary of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I read an extensive -- a group of paragraphs or a whole portion of a statement, I usually get a copy, put it before the witness. When I use -- when I discuss a phrase or one sentence. Up to this point I haven't placed -- one sentence before, which is the exact same thing that the other counsel do too, when it's one sentence or just a couple of sentences. I'd be happy to, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It appears to me that the objection of the Defence is that it is not correctly paraphrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll read the two sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to read these two sentences to you: "I subsequently informed the president of the Crisis Staff about this, as well as Mr. Todorovic and some other members of the Crisis Staff who were present."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's on page P141 ter, page 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, at this point, I believe it's quite obvious, because the question, the way it was posed, suggested that Mr. Zaric advised. This is what my colleague said. And now when he quotes that he said "I informed," this is a difference, a very significant difference, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he did not set up the Crisis Staff, but rather the president, Stevan Todorovic, and some members, in that month you were talking about, not the institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I didn't say anything about setting up the Crisis Staff. The question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we get on? The sentence has been read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you present in the room, sir, at a second radio interview when Simo Zaric -- or did Simo Zaric at that second radio interview tell you and the others in the room that he had informed the president of the Crisis Staff, Stevan Todorovic, and other members of the Crisis Staff about the proposals of the Odzak officials relating to exchanges? Were you present for that, or do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an employee of the centre at that time, and I don't think there was any reason for Simo Zaric to tell me what he did and where he was, because I was not an official of the secretariat for National Defence for him to tell me that. So I have no idea where he was or who he talked to. I was not familiar with that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, during that second conversation, Simo Zaric says that he informed -- I'm sorry, he informs the Odzak officials that he had put the proposals to the Crisis Staff, and they had, in principle, nothing against an all-for-all type of exchange. Do you recall that conversation between Simo Zaric and the Odzak officials during that second radio communication? Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall. Yesterday I told you what I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to disbelieve Simo Zaric's statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that the Crisis Staff would not oppose an all-for-all exchange? Are you aware of any bias or prejudice which would prevent him from telling the truth relating to that subject?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't state anything in relation to whether he would say either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. My question to you is: Are you aware of any bias or prejudice? I'm not asking you about the particular statement itself, the validity of it; just any bias or prejudice which would prevent him from saying something -- that something -- or which would make him say something that was not true.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about any prejudice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Finally, the issue of the Crisis Staff has come up in this case. Were you aware who the members of the Crisis Staff were, any of them?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about Stevan Todorovic and Savo Popovic. I haven't heard -- I haven't read anywhere all the members of the Crisis Staff listed, and I don't know according to which criteria the Crisis Staff was formed, so I didn't know who their members were. I did hear that these two were members.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you really weren't aware of much about the Crisis Staff, since you really weren't interested in politics, so you weren't politically involved in Samac, or anywhere else; it just didn't interest you?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was never at the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Re-examination, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No re-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Simic, for giving evidence to the Trial Chamber. We are now finished. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we're waiting for the next witness, would it be an appropriate time to tender the translation of P170, which was the diagram that Mr. Sarkanovic drew last week? I've provided a copy to my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Hopefully they've had a chance to look at the three little boxes on the page. Unless there's any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I formally tender into evidence a translation of P170 into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have confirmation?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P170 ter and P170.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we can proceed and bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning, and please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes. The counsel examining the witness. Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Savic.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So that we can have a swift and easy testimony, can you please tell me first: Do you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If you have any problem with communication, that you can't hear me, please let me know so that we can prevent any problems. If I ask you a question that you don't understand, please let me know so that I can repeat that question, et cetera. Considering that you and I are speaking the same language and that we understand each other, I would ask you if you could wait a couple of seconds before you answer my question so that we can allow some time for the interpreters and the Trial Chamber and all the participants in the proceedings can hear what I asked and what you answered, so that everything is properly entered into the transcript. So that your testimony is favourably reproduced as you are testifying.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: First of all, for the record, can you please tell the Trial Chamber your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: My name is Jovo Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When were you born, and where?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 21st of May, 1949, in Gornja Slatina, municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is that in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about your schooling.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I completed a grammar school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where did you complete the grammar school?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: In Gradacac, in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: What are you doing now?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I'm an officer of the army of Republika Srpska. I'm currently assistant commander for logistics at the infantry brigade, which is based in Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me your rank?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I'm a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm married. I have two daughters and a granddaughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where are you and your family living now?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I live in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Since when have you been living in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of May, 1975.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you serve in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I served in the Yugoslav People's Army, at the school for reserve officers in Bileca, in 1974, and in 1975 I was on work practice, which was part of the education, in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you finished your military service, what was the rank when you left the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: At that time I was lieutenant, second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And when you returned with the reserve second lieutenant of the Yugoslav People's Army, where were you positioned? Rather, where was your military schedule? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I first worked at the secretariat for National Defence in Samac municipality, but I was in Derventa, at the reserve unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This unit in Derventa, that is Yugoslav People's Army unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether that unit was part of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: No. I was in a war unit. Of course, members of that unit were reserve troops, and according to the needs, they were engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was your rank immediately before the hostilities broke out in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: At that time I was Captain First Class.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the meetings that were held with the reserve officers of the Yugoslav People's Army in the memorial home, Mitra Trifunovic, in Samac, and did you go to these meetings? Could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do not recall the date. I think it was in December 1991. I received an invitation from -- or a call from the secretariat of National Defence, the relevant organ, to go to the memorial home, to the meeting. The following invitation or call was the same. And immediately after new year, in January 1992, was again to go to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, let us come back to that very first meeting that was held at the end of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please approach his microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who were the people who were invited to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: All reserve officers were called to that meeting, officers and non-commissioned officers, from the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were there present there members of people from -- of Croatian ethnicity, Muslim ethnicity, all other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This meeting was attended by Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. There were many of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall who spoke at this meeting and who addressed you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: At this meeting, it was Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic who addressed the attendees. He introduced himself and the immediate members of his command, and then we introduced ourselves to him. Our names, surnames, and ranks. This was an introductory part. He greeted us and said that -- expressed his satisfaction that he saw so many of us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: At that meeting, what did Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic say to those who attended the meeting, the officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, reserve officers?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Except for this introductory part that I told you about, he told us about a very complex political and security situation in Yugoslavia, with a particular focus on Bosnia-Herzegovina. I remember well that he told us that the Yugoslav People's Army had to withdraw to Bosnia-Herzegovina, or its parts, that the commands of units were dispositioned in the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they had a task, that they had a role of -- then JNA that he belonged to had the role to prevent, at any cost, war breaking out in this area and to prevent conflict situations in the territory, and particularly in its area of responsibility, and to enable life of the citizens and their work. That was the general lines. I don't remember everything, but that was what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned conflict situations earlier, was this relating to -- was this to do with interethnic conflict or anything else?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will say what it was. He said that the parties that came to power in 1990, these were nationalistic parties, and they were arming their members. They were doing this in an illegal way, and so on. They were doing it in all manner of ways. And that these relations, interethnic relations, were very tense, and that there was a possibility, since this category of people had the weapons, he said - and I remember the words - the weapons will speak out sooner or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... my learned friend and to the witness. Your Honour, page 31, line 11, we heard that this witness said: "National parties," not "nationalistic." So just a correction to the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pisarevic, maybe you can correct that with the witness. Because we've always had this problem of national parties or nationalistic parties. Can we have that cleared?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic say? Was it national or nationalistic parties?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Nationalist parties, nationalistic parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were there any requests that he expressed towards your officers, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: He wanted us to join the units, of course, according to our possibilities, abilities, specialities, to simply put ourselves at the disposal of JNA units, so that they would have us as their staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, this call was addressed to all the members present there, of all ethnicities, all those who were officers, reserve officers, as reserve non-commissioned officers of the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: What happened at the next meeting which was held?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: At the next meeting, immediately after new year, again we were called, but at this time there were far fewer people who attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who did not come to this second meeting that was held, also at the memorial home? Can you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Far fewer members came, that is, far fewer Muslims and Croats, and I think that all the Serbs came.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know the reason why, at this second meeting, fewer Muslims and Croats attended?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I think - and this is just my opinion - that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, we don't want the opinion. If the witness doesn't know the reasons, then he doesn't know. We don't want his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You have heard the suggestion of the Presiding Judge. Do you know the reasons or you don't know the reasons?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I just assume the reasons. I don't know the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You don't need to answer. Can you tell us: What happened in that next meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: At the next meeting, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, together with his assistant for personnel, said, among other things, that he had taken a decision that in the town of Samac there should be a unit established and that its name would be the 4th Detachment, and would be part of the Tactical Group 17, 17th Tactical Group, that is, it would be made up of JNA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And was this order issued?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did this decision about the establishment of the 4th Detachment of the Yugoslav People's Army as part of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA, what did it contain?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, I recall some parts of this order, and certain officers were appointed to command posts, name, surname, and rank was given; their role, their task of the newly formed unit, and it was, I would say, similar to the role of the JNA. But it was slightly given in a more detailed way. This unit was established. And it said that it would have to prevent the escalation of war or the transfer of war from Republic of Croatia to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, of Posavina, that is, of the town of Samac. Of course, in this order, Bosnia-Herzegovina wasn't mentioned, but it mentioned Posavina, its area of responsibility, and the town of Samac. Apart from that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Apart from that, the tasks of the detachment were to provide normal life in the town of Samac, to prevent interethnic conflicts, possible interethnic conflicts, to enable and provide normal work for the companies, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this order, did Commander Nikolic also determine the territorial area of responsibility of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the area?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: With this order, it gave the area of responsibility, defined it, and that was - and I'm talking about the border - that would be to the right, that would be the bridge on the Sava River; to the left, the bridge on the Bosna; and straight on, the bridge between the Sava River and Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understood, that was the local commune of the town of Samac; that was the area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In this order, who was appointed as the commander of the 4th Detachment of Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The commander was Mr. Radovan Antic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And to which command post were you appointed?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed as the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Simo Zaric? What was he appointed as at that command?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simo Zaric was appointed as the assistant commander for intelligence and security of the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of appointment did Mr. Miroslav Tadic get at that time at the command?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miroslav Tadic was appointed as the assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Mehmed Vukovic, Lieutenant Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lieutenant Mehmed Vukovic was appointed as the operations officer at the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber: How did it proceed, the bringing up manpower levels for this detachment? How did people join in and what did the command do?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The establishment levels of the 4th Detachment went through the then secretariat for National Defence. They called up military recruits. They informed them about their military schedules and sent them to the unit, that is, they would just give them their schedule and explain where the location was and to whom they should report in case of mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did the command work as to receiving new recruits?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: We from the command had the obligation to accept people who would report to the unit, to tell them to which lower-echelon unit they should go, to whom they should report, et cetera, to which commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This process of bringing up manpower levels of the 4th Detachment, how long did it go on for?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: This is a longer process. I don't know how long this took, but people did respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me now: What was the internal organisation of the 4th Detachment, and what did that entail?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment had the command, the command of the detachment, it had quartermaster's squad, department, which is more or less logistics, then it had a medical department, and also a reconnaissance squad. Apart from that, that would be the most important part, and then there were also the -- there were four companies. There were four infantry companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that this is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our break and continue at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You can hear me, can't you, Mr. Savic? Before the break, you spoke about the organisational structure of the 4th Detachment. Tell me, please: What did a company consist of in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Each of the infantry companies had a commander, assistant commander, or rather, deputy commander, and then the lower-ranking units of organisation were platoons and departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: These platoons and squads, did they have their own commanders?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Even the lowest-ranking unit had a commander. And then the squad had its own commander, the platoon had its own commander, and then the company, which was the highest-ranking among these units had its own commander and a deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain the procedure. How were commanders of squads, platoons, and companies named, or rather, appointed, and who had the authority to appoint them?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The detachment and company commanders were appointed by a decision of the commander of the 17th Tactical Group. As for lower-ranking units, platoons and squads, those commanders were appointed by the detachment command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: These platoon commanders and squad commanders, did they need to have any military ranks? Was that a military position or an officer's position?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: As far as the platoon is concerned, it could be a commissioned officer or a non-commissioned officer. At squad level, it could have been a soldier or a soldier with a military rank, a lance corporal or a private first class, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was there a communications platoon?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: No, there was a communications squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Tell me, please: How many members of the 4th Detachment were there between the 5th of January and the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I kept records of that, and we had a person who was in charge of administrative things. We made lists according to name and rank. I remember that there were 452 members.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can you tell us something about the ethnic make-up or, rather, structure of the members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Serbs were the predominant group in the 4th Detachment, and there were a number of Muslims too, a considerable number of Muslims, and fewer Croats. But there were also persons there who referred to themselves as Yugoslavs. Other ethnic groups were represented too, to a minor extent, admittedly, Albanians, Macedonians, but only very few.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Among the commissioned officers or, rather, commanders of the infantries, we heard that there was a Muslim commander already, but among the commanders of platoons and squads, were Muslims and Croats represented also among those, in addition to Serbs, of course?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were Muslims who were commanders. Even the company commander, the platoon commander, squad commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us now, please, where was the command of the 4th Detachment based, located?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: It was in the Sit company building in Edvarda Kardelja Street. I'm not sure about the number. I think it was 20 or thereabouts, but that's not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you have at your disposal in terms of accommodation, in terms of accommodating the command at the Sit factory?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: We had a rather large working room, which housed the admin section, and we had another small room for communications officers and communications equipment, radio sets mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now that you've mentioned communications equipment, which communications equipment did the 4th Detachment have?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: A wireless radio, more specifically, RUP 2B. It's very difficult for me to remember the exact names of the equipment, because I'm not a communications officer myself, but I know it was an RUP set.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe this RUP radio set, the technical details, its weight, its size, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: You can carry it on your back, but usually communications officers carry it on their chest, because the control panel is there. You can establish a link with the Superior Command using that kind of equipment. I think it's about ten kilos in terms of weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the detachment only had one such radio set.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And it was at the command?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in that small room.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Outside the command, were there any symbols that were prominent and easily visible?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when you approach the building from the side of the street, there were two symbols or two flags. One was the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the other was the Yugoslav flag, the flag of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment was set up, and so on and so forth. Tell me: How, and in what way, did members of the detachment sign for their weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of lists that had already been made, we planned some sort of training, which was eventually carried out in the village of Potocari, near Brcko. We organised the transport of our members there to that site by bus. That's where they signed for weapons or equipment, equipment which came from the command of the 17th Tactical Group. In that same training ground, we had target practice from artillery weapons [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that there is some misunderstanding here in the transcript. On page 40, line 7 he said: "We had target practice from artillery weapons." Artillery weapons were not mentioned by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have that clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What sort of weapons, what sort of target practice did you have? What weapons were you using for practice?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Merely automatic rifles, infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Not artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Not artillery weapons, no, by no means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You referred to this training group in the village of Potocari. Was that an official training ground for the training of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After this training, members of the 4th Detachment, did they eventually sign for these infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment, what did it have in terms of military weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment had infantry weapons, including rifles, automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles, machine-guns, hand-held launchers. That's what our unit had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Members of the detachment, did they sign for any other kind of equipment, gas masks or uniforms or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A considerable number of our members had gas masks at home, because we had assignments to war units, so we kept these things at home. At the training ground, those who didn't have any or those who had not yet signed for any of those received them there at the training ground. The uniforms were olive-drab. Up to that point I had not seen camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say "SMB," or rather, olive-drab, were these uniforms usually and normally worn by the JNA, with all the insignia?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. This SMB olive-drab uniform was the official JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When one signed for weapons, was this procedure -- did this procedure entail certain documents, the giving of certain documents to members of the detachment when they signed for a weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Each and every one of us had to put their signature there, in order to certify what they had taken or received. There was a certificate stating the name, the number, the serial number of the rifle, the number of bullets received, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: As far as the quartermaster's equipment was concerned, a different kind of document was drawn up, the reverse -- the receipt.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Exhibit D48/4 ter. Can you please have a look and then we'll discuss this document.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Hold on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please put this on the ELMO so that the accused can see the document too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You have looked at this document now. Can you please tell us: What is it, really?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: This document is a document where a conscript or a member of the detachment signs for a weapon, a weapon given him at that moment. I remember this too. If I may just be allowed. Every rifle, automatic or semi-automatic rifle, and any other kind of weapon, when it was distributed, each time you were given a rifle, you would get a combat set and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read what it says in the upper-left corner. Which unit is this? Which unit issued this?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Military post TG 17, confidential number 943-1/9, date, the 1st of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, the title, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: "Military post."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. The one just below.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: "Approval for bearers of" -- I'm afraid I can't read this. It's a bit blurry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This thing here.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: "Permit or approval for carrying weapons."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who it was signed by and what the stamp is?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel -- Commander Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The way I understand this, this means that members of the 4th Detachment were armed and could only receive permit from the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment, did they have their own warehouses where they could store weapons and military equipment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment had no storage rooms or warehouses. We only had one rather large room and another very small one which was used by communications officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: From where did you obtain all the weapons and equipment you needed for members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: All weapons and equipment for the 4th Detachment was obtained from a logistics organ of the command of the 17th Tactical Group in Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did a member of the 4th Detachment receive instructions from the command pertaining to the keeping and the carrying of the weapons they had signed for? If so, please tell us exactly what instructions those were.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Each member of the 4th Detachment who signed for any kind of rifle was told, was ordered, to take good care of how they were using the weapon. It was out of the question to use the weapon until specifically ordered by someone, or rather, by their direct superior. In addition to that, we ordered or, rather, instructed people that weapons were to be kept at home but separate from the ammo, for safety reasons. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did every member have the obligation to also carry this permit if they were carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Every time they carried weapons, every member had the obligation to also have on them this specific document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We shall no longer require this document for the time being. You can take it back. Thank you. The 4th Detachment was set up. Please tell me: How was life organised for the members of the 4th Detachment? Was that some sort of barracks life, life in the barracks, or was it organised in a different way? Can you please tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: We, members of the 4th Detachment, went about our daily business and tasks. We did not have a proper barracks. All we had was the room that I told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Members of the 4th Detachment, if they had to go away somewhere from where they lived, from Bosanski Samac, did they need to have any sort of permit or certificate in order to be able to travel?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: No. That was not necessary at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Which means the command never knew exactly the numerical strength of the detachment at any given point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
