utterances.text: It was difficult to tell, because people kept travelling. They worked somewhere he would, they would come and go, and they lived in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Just another question in relation to that. Members of the detachment, did they receive any compensation or, rather, salary, because they were members of the 4th Detachment, whether they were members of the command or members of the army, or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I am positive, and I can confirm that neither I nor anyone else from the unit ever received any compensation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were there occurrences where members of the detachment, in contravention of an order, were using infantry weapons that they had signed for? If so, if any occurrences are known to you, please tell us what you know about that.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I remember two cases, we called it misuse. One of the members, a man I knew quite well, in a drunken state, assumed the right to take his rifle out to the garden and fire a bullet or two. We reported this to the commander of the Tactical Group, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, and the assistant for security, using his own channels, informed the security organ or, rather, body of the command of the Tactical Group. After that, military police came along. They took the weapon away and proceedings were initiated. We would interview such -- this person and we told him -- I think there was another man called Mikerevic, but I'm not sure, and we told both of them that what they had done was not an honourable act and not something a soldier should do, that it was a major infringement and that other such cases should be prevented from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We'll move on to a different subject now. We're talking about the period towards the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, don't move away from your microphone. It's difficult for the interpreters to get what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try as hard as I can. I promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Including the 16th and 17th of April, what was the security situation in Samac municipality, and how did the whole thing look? Was it any different from the way life had gone on before?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is telling me I said: "Until the 16th or the 17th," so we're covering the time period until the 16th and the 17th. I'm talking about the situation in Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What characterised the situation, the overall situation, and in some way disturbed the peaceful life of citizens in Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, in the town of Samac, life changed in relation to the previous year, and especially in relation to the period before that, because we started drifting apart and dividing along ethnic lines: Serbs, Muslims, Croats, and the rest. Acts of sabotage started occurring in the depth of the area. I remember an incident at a cafe, at the Valentino Cafe, where two young men were playing, or sort of toying around with a hand grenade. Both were killed. The girl who was there standing close to them was seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps recall when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall when that happened, because the name of valentine's, that was the 14th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether after that event there was a rally of the citizens at the cinema in Samac? If you recall anything, can you tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do know we had received information. I don't know who was the organiser of the rally, but I know that they asked for someone from the command to come to the cinema hall, and Commander Antic was not around at the time, and myself, as his deputy, ordered Mr. Simo Zaric to go to this rally, to this meeting, because in the meantime, Commander Antic had ordered Mr. Zaric that, apart from his functional duty, he would be also carrying out the duties in relation to morale and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, when the commander, Commander Antic, was not present in the unit or the town, you were the one issuing orders to the other members of the detachment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And precisely because of this, because Commander Antic had ordered Mr. Zaric to carry out the tasks of morale and information, you ordered him to go to this rally?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Zaric report to you about what he said at this rally once he returned? If I understood you correctly, you didn't go to this rally.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not go.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Zaric told me that many people gathered; that, again, in his own element, he called on the people not to raise the tension; that the security, safety, had to be at a high level. And there were other things which I do not recall, but these were the basic things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know about the case of setting up barricades at the entrances into Bosanski Samac? Do you know anything about that? And if so, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One day, I think it was sometime in March, but I'm not sure. It was early spring, I would say, and we received the information that two barricades had been set up by the members of the SDA. One barricade had been set up near the Mebos company, at the entrance to Samac, and the other one on the opposite side, also at the entrance to Samac, and near the Uzarija, not far from Pik company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: These persons at the barricades, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They had Kalashnikovs rifles. Apart from that, they also had set up vehicles as obstacles, and it was not possible to leave the town. For us, this was a shocking situation. How could it be possible for someone not to be able to come from a village into the town? That was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber: How many entrances into Samac were there?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: There are two main entrances into the Samac, and one not so important.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Which one is the third one?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: That is on the Bosna River, and we would call that -- that was the confluence of two rivers, Bosna and Sava River, and there was a small bridge there, a very narrow bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And which village -- or rather, from which village do you come in order to get to Samac across that bridge that you told us about?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: You go to the village of Prud, and then on to other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Which ethnic group lived in the village of Prud?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: In the village of Prud, Croats lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, on that day, anyone called you from the command of the 17th Tactical Group to the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think -- in fact, I don't think, I'm sure that Commander Antic told the commander of the Tactical Group, Stevan Nikolic, and told him this about what was happening to do with barricades, and later he told us not to get involved into this, that a conversation was held with some people, from SUP probably, and that this was within their area of authority, as that we should not get mixed up in this and that we should not get involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, the 4th Detachment did not get involved into this, into lifting of the barricades?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: No, no, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were the barricades removed on that day?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So the barricade was not set up on the entrance to Samac from Prud?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any other events that significantly marked the security situation in Samac? Do you know perhaps about the appearance of a flyer, a leaflet, that Muslims, members of the 4th Detachment, and they were insulted in that leaflet, they were told they should leave the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have that leaflet in your hand?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to read it very quickly. I had it in my hand. I read it. I didn't know much about it. But there was -- concern was raised, because there was a large number of Muslims in the detachment, and this leaflet had this some kind of a list, and there were insults, that they should leave the detachment, they should leave the JNA, and that they should leave this, as it was called, the occupying army, they should go to their own units, established by the SDA party. That's how it was -- that was the general gist of the leaflet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. What happened in the town of Samac after the leaflet appeared? Were there any activities towards the members of the 4th Detachment who were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. I'm not sure about the dates. I remember that our three members, they were in civilian clothes, and they were in their own private vehicle, going through the town, as usual. They had no weapons on them. They were passing by a restaurant near the market, one of the restaurants, and they were shot at by two members, two Muslims, who were members of the reserve police force. Of course, they were party members, and the consequence of that incident, of that excess was that there were two Muslims and a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before we go on, could we just clarify perhaps whether the witness actually saw this, whether he was there or whether it's something he heard of? That's not completely clear in the transcript at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that he had the knowledge, that he knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you an eyewitness to this event?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How do you know about what happened?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: This is a very small community. Shooting was heard. I think I was at home. This is not very far from my home. Suddenly the news spread that someone shot at somebody, and later on I found out who these people were. I knew these people. I don't know what their names are. I forgot their names and surnames. But that's how it was. I did not see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you know that in April, in the area of the village of Batkusa, JNA helicopters brought some military units and paramilitary units --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: -- and a group that came from Krajina? Who did you hear this from? How were you informed? Who met them? How is it they dressed, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I heard this -- I had this information from Commander Antic. He was born in this village, village of Batkusa. He went home and he told me that he was stopped by a patrol at the entrance to his village. His vehicle was searched, checked where he was from, who he was. He didn't know who the people were. They were dressed in camouflage uniforms and had some insignia that he then saw for the first time, had some patches, they had caps and hats they were wearing. And he said that he was a little frightened by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you find anything out from any other sources?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There was talk that in the helicopters they landed on the Batkusa field, that these were specials, members of special units, people who were not from -- they're not locals, but also there were some other young men who were local and who were with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if this group ever became a part of any formation, of any unit of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: No. I know that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You said no. Can you give a full answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Not a single member of this group was a member of the 4th Detachment unit. And I don't know whether they were members of any other units. They were not members of the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to follow their activities in the period after the 16th of April, 1992 as well? What did they do? Under whose command were they, and so on? Do you have any such information?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Well, during that period of time, there was talk that these people were housed in the village of Obudovac, that they went where they want, when they wanted. They came to Samac, putting themselves at the disposal of the then chief of SUP, Mr. Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now we come to the activities of some other citizens, associations, institutions, and so on. Were there any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. I was just waiting to see whether you were going to move on, as in fact you are. I would just like to ask Mr. Savic a question concerning the paramilitaries' arrival in Batkusa. And I'm wondering, Mr. Savic, whether you know who organised for the arrival of these paramilitaries, and albeit that they don't seem to be, as you've said, a member of any military unit, they clearly were on JNA helicopters. So I'm wondering whether you know who organised for their arrival in Batkusa and their transportation using JNA helicopters, if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may answer only about what I heard, and what I heard was that this was organised by the chief, Stevan Todorovic, that their transport and their arrival.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will continue where I broke off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were there any peace rallies of the citizens calling on to interethnic tolerance and peaceful coexistence, considering that there was tension that was being raised in Samac? Were there any other -- were there any such forces that were trying to keep it all together, considering that you were a citizen of Samac, you are a citizen of Samac, and were the people trying to prevent those hostilities that later occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Samac is a small town. We knew each other and saw each other very frequently. Occasionally we had the opportunity to talk to each other about this situation, to exchange our opinions, and anxiety was a daily thing and being raised all the time. A group of citizens from one building - and I knew them all - one day they called me, in the afternoon, if I would come, so that they would show me what kind of barricades they were setting up. Of course, as soon as somebody mentions barricades, then of course the thought is that this is to do something that had already occurred, so I went there and I heard music and song. When I got there, a large number of people and us guests are gathered together with music and song and grill. So they said to me: These were our grill barricades, nothing to do with the SDA barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: These grill barricades, or barbecue barricades, were they organised in other parts of town?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Of course, in my immediate neighbourhood on several occasions, in the other part of town as well, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who participated in these barbecue barricades? What was the ethnic structure?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Everybody who lived nearby, regardless of whether they were Serbs, Muslims, or Croats, or any other ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You certainly remember some rallies, calls for peace, and so on, that were held at some times? You do recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that, but I didn't attend them. I was somewhere in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: But do you remember that there were?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were. There were calls for stopping all divisions, that people should continue to co-exist here, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The concept of the 4th Detachment was precisely as it was expressed by the citizens who called for peace, tolerance, and peaceful coexistence?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you that it was on the basis of that. I was a member of that detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And so now we come -- I'd like you to testify about the events that occurred on the day between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992. Can you tell me: This day, 16th of April, 1992, is there something, are there some events that occurred during that day which set it apart from the other days that had previously gone by?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The 16th of April passed just like the previous day, the 15th of April. It was just an ordinary working day, like any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The behaviour of the members of the 4th Detachment, was it the same as during the previous days? Did you issue any orders or any warning instructions?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Everything was the same except the fact that we had groups of reconnaissance people whose task was to observe the town --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. Do you mean patrols? You're calling patrols reconnaissance people? Should we clarify that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I mean patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: These patrols were given daily tasks by the commander, and their obligation was that one of them should report, either to the commander or to the duty officer, that is, a member of the command of the detachment, about the observed situation, if he noticed something that was outside of the ordinary, that he should inform about that. These were the groups I meant. I'm sorry. I apologise. That was a lapse.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who determined the composition of the patrols, how many members of patrols were there in one patrol and what was their ethnic structure?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The patrols were decided on in the following way: Company commanders, that is, platoon commanders, had the obligation to organise everybody taking three -- from their units and assigning three members of the patrols. Their tasks I've already stated. And these patrol members carried out their tasks with their arms, bearing their arms. The ethnic composition was the same as the detachment composition. There were never three Serbs together or three Croats [Realtime transcript read in error "Serbs"] together or three Muslims. It was always a mixed composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague Mr. Lazarevic says that in line 14, on page 56, should say -- should say Croats, and not Serbs, because Serbs are mentioned twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So let's clarify this. The patrols were never of the same ethnic structure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, you in the command, you deputy commander, you never knew which people were members of the patrol during that evening or that night?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: No. That changed. That was probably known by the direct commander. But I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did this mean that the commander couldn't have known that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps he did know, because they were directly subordinate to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When did the patrol start operating?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Mostly at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was in the command on the 16th of April, in the evening?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Of course, the duty officer, I mean him, and the duty communications officer. I think - in fact, I'm certain - that at that time, that was Stanko Dujkovic. He was a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was the duty communications officer?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: His name was Milenko Ugljesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me: Where were you then in the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: On that date, the 16th, I was asleep, at home, with my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you wake up during that night?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and suddenly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What were you woken by?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Shooting. Shooting. At first I thought someone was again misusing their weapons, and then I opened the window, on the -- from the eastern side of the town, shooting was coming. At the very same moment, because my house was in the immediate vicinity, I got dressed very quickly and I went straight to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please, when you say from the eastern part of the town, is that the part of town known as Donja Mahala?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's it. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is it very close to Donja Mahala that the police building, the TO building, the Municipal Assembly building, and the Trifunovic monument are?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: When I went to the command, because that was near where I lived, I was walking along the street, and my assessment was that the shooting was somewhere in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is this the memorial centre, Mitra Trifunovic? There is no monument; there is the memorial centre.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Once you reached the command, who did you find there? What information did you obtain when you got there?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: A duty officer, the communications officer, and a number of other people, all looking frightened, told me that there was shooting in the SUP area, in the area surrounding the SUP building. They said they didn't have any details, but they also said that they would know shortly probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How many were you there at that moment at the command?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I was among the first to arrive. There were four or five people there when I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What happened then? Did other members of the command begin to arrive, members of the detachment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very soon, within one hour, I think, Radovan Antic and Simo Zaric turned up, not together. I'm not sure who came first. They were all asking the same question: What's happening? What's going on? Radovan, looking worried, we still didn't know anything for sure, and we talked to the people who were patrolling the town, they said there was shooting in such-and-such area, and so on and so forth. And then Radovan tried to get some other information to sort of piece the whole thing together. He used the wireless to call Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, and he talked to him over the radio set. And then after that conversation, he told me to remain at the command, to monitor closely the situation, and to wait for further orders. He and Simo Zaric had been ordered by the commander of the Tactical Group to immediately go to Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was that an order by Commander Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So between -- ever since Antic left for Pelagicevo, you were, to all intents and purposes, the commander there?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Of course, in his absence, I was there as commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did people gather? How many people came to the command? For example, by 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: This is a very difficult question to answer. We're talking about figures here. I'd say around 90 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: -- 20. Those who were patrolling the town, and then they woke some other people up to go and check the situation to see what was going on, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that one of those 20 people who came was also Fadil Topcagic?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him at the office, what I refer to as the working room, and then I told Simo and Antic what had happened to him [as interpreted]. He was visibly frightened and agitated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I believe that we have some misunderstanding here in the transcript. On page 60, line 6. "And then I told Simo and Antic what had happened to him." No. It was actually Fadil Topcagic who said to the witness that he said to Antic and Zaric what happened to him. This was the meaning of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have it clarified?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: There is some misunderstanding in the transcript. What did Fadil Topcagic tell you exactly? Who did he tell what?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: He says: Now, on my way in, I met Simo and Radovan, and I told him briefly what had happened to him [as interpreted]. What had happened to me, what had happened to him. And then he told me slowly and gradually the whole story at the office. I'm not sure if I was clear enough this time around.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Again we have the same problem: And I told not him. I told them briefly what happened to me. This is Fadil Topcagic speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who did he tell this? Who did Fadil Topcagic tell this?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Hold on a second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness use names. So-and-so told A or B or C. Can he use names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please don't use personal pronouns: We, they, us, them, you. Please use names. Who did Fadil Topcagic talk to? Who did he tell what had happened to them when he met them at the entrance to the command?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Fadil Topcagic met Mr. Simo Zaric and Mr. Radovan Antic, who were about to leave for Pelagicevo, as they had been ordered. They met at the entrance. And then Fadil told Simo and Radovan very briefly what had happened to Fadil, but very briefly, in passing. And then just after that, they left, Simo and Radovan left for Pelagicevo. And Fadil told me what had happened to Fadil. Does this make it any better now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Thank you. When Fadil Topcagic told you about this, to you personally, were there any other people present at the command?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were other people there. Some people were just sitting and some others were just listening to see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please testify before the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can counsel please be asked to speak closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: -- as to what Fadil Topcagic exactly told you about what had happened to him between the 16th and the 17th?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: He told me that during the night a police officer came along, a police officer named Savo Savic, and another man whom he didn't know. The other man was wearing camouflage uniform. They told him that the two Savics and the unknown man, that Fadil was supposed it take them to show where Crkvina was, the village of Crkvina. When Fadil got there, someone - now, whether it was the man who accompanied him who went in the same direction or not - ordered that a group of masked people or, rather, people wearing camouflage uniforms, be taken to Samac, to show where the SUP building was and where the municipal building was. He did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he say that anyone was wounded during that operation?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did he tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: There was a wounded man, and he took him to the medical station, Crkvina or Samac; I'm not sure where.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point, since the departure for Pelagicevo, did the commander of the 4th Detachment, Radovan Antic, get through to you, through -- over the radio? If so, when precisely? And did he give you any specific orders? If so, which orders, from Commander Antic?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Commander Antic called me on the radio and he said: Simo and I are starting out from Pelagicevo and are on our way back to Samac. Prepare and summon members of the command, and company commanders. I'll be there in a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I used the group of people who were near me, and I sent them to the town of Samac, to inform and call people. We had this organised. It was part of the preparation for our unit. We just call each other. I'd call Marko, Marko would call me, and so on and so forth. So they went to the town to look for commanders mainly, and the command of the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you also call members of the detachment, those who you could reach?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And when Antic and Zaric arrived, when was that? What time was it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: This is a bit of a tall order, asking me about the time of day, but I think it was about 8.00 in the morning perhaps, half past 7.00, 8.00, thereabouts. I'm not sure, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How many members of the 4th Detachment were gathered, were assembled, by that time? How many came to the command of the 4th Detachment, or rather, outside the Sit building?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: By 8.00, I believe there were about 50 people assembled, 50, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This procedure continued, the process of calling people up, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Zaric and Mr. Antic came back, what were you told about what Commander Nikolic had told them?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: When Radovan and Simo came back, Radovan assembled those present, members of the command, and another commander who was there, and one of the regular soldiers, and he told us about what had been discussed with Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic. He told us, in addition to other things, that Lieutenant Colonel had already talked to someone from the municipality, asked what was going on, allegedly, and then went on to tell Radovan: Go to Samac. Mobilise your unit. Mobilise your detachment and wait for further instructions and orders. That's what Radovan told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Commander Antic, did he tell you then whether Commander Nikolic had told him who had taken control of the town or that key facilities and institutions had been taken, the SUP, the municipality, the post office?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed he told me that a Serbian municipality had been set up, headed by a Crisis Staff, something along these lines, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Did he tell you which armed units -- who the people with the weapons were who had taken the police building, the municipal building, the post office, the memorial centre, the radio station?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I forgot about that. I thought that's what you were referring to. Yes, he did inform us that people, members of special units, had taken, in addition to the municipal building and the SUP building, also the memorial centre and the Pik factory building, the post office, some companies, the radio station, all the key facilities and institutions had been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The command of the 4th Detachment, during the day, during the 17th, did they receive any orders from the command of the 17th Tactical Group concerning any further activities to be undertaken by the 4th Detachment in its area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What exactly?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The order was that the people who arrived in the unit should be deployed about the -- along the fringes of the town, and this meant the defensive embankments on the right bank of the River Sava and on the right bank of the River Bosna. Radovan Antic told me that he would take care of this personally. He gathered people. We had lists with names belonging to certain units, and he personally took them there and deployed them along those defensive positions. I stayed back at the command. People kept coming in, and I was there to meet them, and this did go on for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: At the same time, as people were being deployed along the defensive embankments that you spoke about, people from the 4th Detachment, were there any other activities under way concerning collection of weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: That was a different order. I remember that an order came along for the remaining people, the remaining men who were coming in and reporting, to wait. They would have the task to start collecting illegally owned weapons of military origin in an organised manner. When Commander Antic came back, at some point in the afternoon, after he had completed that part of the task, again he told me: Stay here. I'll take some people along and take care of that. And then he left off. Prior to that, commanders who were coming in and people who were coming in were ordered by him to us at the command and the members with regard to procedures surrounding the activity to be undertaken, he sternly warned everyone against entering people's flats or houses in an arbitrary manner, that nothing was to be seized but, rather, the only thing that was to be collected were weapons of military origin. And from those people who were not in possession of the relevant documents. And that's exactly what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When did the members of the 4th Detachment occupy those lines of defence?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Radovan took them there about 10.00, I think, and he was back in the afternoon, about 3.00 in the afternoon, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us, roughly: When was it ordered that members of the 4th Detachment along the lines of defence should be given white armbands as instinctive marks, of members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you the date. What I can tell you is that there was an order for every member of the 4th Detachment to wear a white armband on the left upper arm or the left shoulder strap, which was an insignia of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was the first night that the members of the 4th Detachment spent at their positions?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The night between the 17th and the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were they already wearing white armbands during that night?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Weapons collection, how long did that take?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: It lasted in the afternoon hours of the 17th and the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Which next day?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Commander Antic determine exactly who would monitor the way his order was being implemented, his order concerning the collection of military infantry weapons that were turned over of people's own free will?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: In addition to giving crystal clear instructions to all those participating in the operation, Radovan Antic also ordered members of the command to closely monitor the implementation, and if there was an incident of some kind, to immediately report either to him or to me. We had prepared everything that was necessary for the implementation, for the safety of those participating, in order to continue that the whole thing goes through smoothly. And on that day - I'm speaking of the 17 - there were no incidents of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were there any incidents on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: No. On the 18th --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe there is something that is not quite clear here in the transcript, on page 67, line 2. The witness said he also ordered members of the command, and here we have commander and then after that Radovan Antic, so maybe my colleague can clarify that, but it's quite obvious what the witness was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that can be cleared.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: To which members of the command did the commander of the 4th Detachment order to monitor closely the implementation of his order related to the voluntary collection of weapons that had been turned over voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Members of the command were --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who did he order this to precisely?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Simo Zaric. This other man -- the people who were there, those were the people he ordered. There were a few other people there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did he appoint a number of monitors or just Mr. Zaric, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely. I often tend to forget. Tadic, Zaric, and he himself. He was some sort of a nexus, a link, because he was supposed to monitor them and they were supposed to monitor the activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So this operation, collection of military weapons voluntarily turned over by citizens who had been in possession of that, was it completed on the 18th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me: Why was it necessary to carry out this operation, a collection of weapons, the voluntary collection of infantry weapons of military origin?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before he answers, I object to my learned friend Mr. Pisarevic's continued use of the word "voluntary." That's very much in dispute in the case and he's leading the witness there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is the case for the Defence. We had this evidence even with the previous witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm objecting to my learned friend using the word "voluntary" in his questions, because it's a leading question, suggesting the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes. By counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Pisarevic will avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can try to avoid that, but, Your Honours, frankly, the whole line of reasoning of the Defence is that these weapons were seized in such a way that upon the invitation of members of the 4th Detachment, the citizens would bring and turn over these weapons of their own free will, members of the 4th Detachment did not search houses, garages, flats, or cars in order to seize these weapons. That's our submission, and this is something that we are trying to prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic, but that is the evidence which must come from the witnesses, not from you, as counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: What was the procedure used by the members of the 4th Detachment as they went about collecting weapons of military origin in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the order, as I've already explained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can this be clarified whether it was the witness who actually saw this or whether it was something the witness heard, and if so, what was the source of his information? The evidence so far has been it was Mr. Tadic and Zaric and Antic who coordinated this. He can talk about the procedure he knew of or what he saw, but if it's hearsay, please, the source is very necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure Mr. Pisarevic will ask the witness about his basis of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you, did you, did you, as you went about collecting weapons, were you in a position to see how this was done, where it was being done?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: No, personally, I was not in a position to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And do you know why the order was issued for these weapons to be collected?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: It was for safety and security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Such as?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Firstly, weapons illegally owned can be misused. Secondly, people deployed along the lines of defence, members of the detachment, were quite close to those houses. Someone might have a blackout, as they say, and might just start shooting and killing people who were deployed there. And last but not least, no one can be allowed to be in possession of military weapons without the proper and relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a convenient time for a break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume our proceedings at 12.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, could you tell this Trial Chamber: When did firing start in Samac and operations, and who undertook these? Which military units?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you. On the same day, the 17th, while Radovan was taking people to the lines, one of our members, Cvijetin Savic, was injured in the stomach with a sniper's bullet from the area of Slavonia, that is, it came from the Sljunkara area. This is what we call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: While you're speaking about Slavonia, could you explain where Slavonia is, in which state?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Slavonia is a part of the Republic of Croatia, and we call that across the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: After that, a couple of minutes later, artillery shelling started, and shells from Slavonia started arriving, as well as from the village of Prud. This was mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. These operations continued on the 18th, and from then on?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on a daily basis, and they were becoming more intensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was there an armed attack on the lines of the Samac town, or rather, on the lines where the members of the 4th Detachment were?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you know about it.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: From the area of the village of Prud, there was in fact an attempt to launch an infantry attack. Of course, our soldiers repelled the attack, and a couple of enemy soldiers remained on the bridge of the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Which army launched this attack, under whose command was it? What was it called?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: This was the army of the Croatian Defence Council from Herceg-Bosna. We call that Croatian Defence Council of Posavina, of Bosnian Posavina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please. Microphone, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, your microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me. There is something which is confusing me. On page 71, line 23, answer: "This was the army of the Croatian Defence Council from Herceg-Bosna. We call that Croatian Defence Council of Posavina, of Bosnian Posavina." Could that be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: Members of which army tried to launch the attack, or rather, launched the attack on the defence lines of the Samac town. What was the army called, what was the state called they belonged to, and who was their command?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Croatian Defence Council belonged to the Croatian people. That's what their army was called. They were from Bosnia-Herzegovina and they called themselves Herceg-Bosna, and this part where Prud was, they called themselves - I heard it from them before - and they said they were members of the Croatian Defence Council of Bosnian Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That was not the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: No. They had at the time their own army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say "they," who do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but these were just members of the Croatian Defence Council. These were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether at that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina there was also the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, was it the one which had the Supreme Command over the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you please testify here to the fact on whether, on the 17th, some armoured vehicles appeared in the part near the defence lines of the 4th Detachment, if you know anything about that, could you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I know that in the afternoon hours, two APCs arrived. These vehicles were sent by the command of the 17th Tactical Group in the event that our troops were at risk on the line. They were sent as assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: These APCs, these were not tanks?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: No. These were APCs. We called this type of vehicle BOV, a BOV vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a characteristic difference between an APC and a tank?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: It's quite a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: These APCs have wheels, and they are armoured vehicles, while the tanks have a different --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: -- while the tanks were on caterpillars and armed with different type of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer. You spoke quite quickly and the interpreters didn't catch it. What is the difference between an APC, that is, a BOV vehicle, and a tank? And can you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The main difference, significant difference between a tank and an APC is that the APCs of the BOV type are on wheels, while a tank is on caterpillars, and of course the difference is in the type of weapons. A tank has a cannon, while a BOV has an anti-aircraft gun of a lower calibre, a 20-millimetre calibre, while the tank has a cannon of 85-millimetre or a hundred millimetre, again, depending what type of tank it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us whether tanks appeared as support? Just a moment. Just slow down. Did tanks appear in the town of Samac? How did they appear? Who sent them, and under whose command were they, and where were they located?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The following day, on the 18th, in the evening hours, again from the command of the 17th Tactical Group, two tanks arrived, and they were deployed on two locations. One tank was located next to the bridge of the Bosna -- on the Bosna River, in the immediate vicinity thereof, and the other tank was located on the crossroads near the Pik Silos, that is, near Uzarija. They were sent on the order of the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, with the purpose of bringing assistance to the troops on the defence lines. In the event of an attack, their task was to fire and to prevent the enemy from attacking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. This tank that you located near Uzarija, was that in the immediate vicinity of the bridge on the Sava River, between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: This is a bridge perhaps two or three kilometres from where it was located. It was there in the event of the Croatian army using that direction. That was its task.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You did not answer one part of my question, and that was: What was the day when this attack of the Croatian Defence Council happened on the members of the 4th Detachment on the Bosna River? Could you tell us the date? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Infantry attack, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These tanks, were they under the command of the 4th Detachment or did they have their own command, and did they have their own crews, and who was -- who commanded these tanks?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The tanks had their own commander. His name was Radomir Zivanvic. He was a major. The crews had communication lines with him at any time, and the use of tanks was only within his remit of that major.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We spoke about the military situation and the position of the 4th Detachment, and so on. Did you and the command of the 4th Detachment have any knowledge about the behaviour of the volunteers from the Serb police regarding arrests and some other activities in the town of Samac? That is, what do you know, starting from the 17th, 18th, and so on, and days that followed? What was happening in the town, inside the town? What do you know about that, and how do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I know that people complained to me. They came to me, asking for assistance, saying they were having problems with the multicoloured ones, as we call them, the specials, so to speak, that they were moving around the town, they were arresting people, snatching weapons from people, of any origin, they were taking vehicles. In a nutshell, the impression was that these people, these specials, were outside of anyone's control, that nobody could touch them. They were doing whatever they wanted, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any cases when members of the 4th Detachment were arrested?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I do recall that among those arrested were also members of our unit, the 4th Detachment. There were civilians who were arrested, citizens, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: To which ethnic group did these members and these other people belong to?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: There were Muslims, Croats, and even Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did you find out that members of the 4th Detachment, non-Serb members of the 4th Detachment, were arrested? Where did you get this information from, and what did command undertake, accordingly?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Simply, the commander of the unit informed us that some of the members did not come to duty, that somebody had been arrested, taken to the SUP, and this is from then on, nobody knew what had happened to him. I said that the majority of people who were arrested were Muslims, Croats, and there was a small number of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And when you found out on the 17th, on the 18th, that certain members of the 4th Detachment were arrested, did the command undertake any steps? What did they do, if anything? What activities followed? Were these people released? How were they released? Who released them?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The command tried, and very frequently succeeded, in bringing these people back from the prison and back into the unit. I know that Simo Zaric's son-in-law or brother-in-law, he also had been arrested, just like some others. I know this because I know the man. Then Commander Antic ordered his officer, assistant for security matters, Simo Zaric, to use his chain of command to inform the Superior Command, and then to try and bring people back from prison, those who were members of the unit. I also know that Radovan Antic also reported to the commander of the Tactical Group about these things, and Commander Nikolic said to Commander Antic: I spoke to Stiv. Go where they are detained. Send Simo to bring them and send them to the units. And that's what Simo did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify a little. So Mr. Zaric was ordered by Commander Antic to go to the police and take members of the 4th Detachment who were not Serbs but were detained in the police [Realtime transcript read in error].

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe we need some clarification of the transcript, because the question here on page 77, line 20, "Mr. Zaric was ordered by Commander Antic to go to the police station and take members of the 4th Detachment who were in the Serbs who were not Serbs but were detained." Just there is a few more words that do not belong here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel can simply repeat his question slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Which ethnicity were members of the 4th Detachment that were arrested for whom Mr. Zaric went to the police station in order to bring them back to the unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind the situation that you described, what else was undertaken by the command of the 4th Detachment in order to somehow help and protect the citizens of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: At the command of the detachment, we had information on a daily basis. We would assess the situation and undertake measures. But we were not strong enough. We didn't have enough strong holds in the organs, specifically in the SUP. And then we tried to use some ways, what we were able to do, to the extent that we were able to do, which was to write a text, as an announcement, to read that, to have this read on the radio, of the local Samac radio, and I know that Simo Zaric, Radovan Antic, and I was involved a little. We wrote a text, thinking that in this way we would soften the situation, we would assist the citizens, in order to have a normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be given D28/4 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, can you please look at the document and then we can discuss this and I can ask a couple of questions in relation to this document. You don't have to read in the entirety.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I know this text. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you -- have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: This one I just looked. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where did you see it? On which occasion? When?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: At the command of the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is this the text that the command that Mr. Zaric compiled together with you and Mr. Antic?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is this the text that commander of the 4th Detachment approved for it to be read out on the local Samac radio?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he even said to Simo: Have this forwarded as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: On the local Samac radio, did you hear that this was read out?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I will now ask you just to read the title, what's typed here in capital letters. To whom is this addressed, the command of the 4th Detachment, who are they addressing?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Citizens of Bosanski Samac, Muslims, Croats, Serbs, Yugoslavs, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Muslims, Croats, and Serbs, we won't discuss. What does this mean, "Yugoslavs"? Who were these citizens of Bosanski Samac that you were addressing as Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yugoslavs were people, citizens of Bosanski Samac, who declared themselves as such. Also in pre-electoral activities, or generally, these people would say: I'm a Yugoslav. And that's all. These were these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that citizens of the former Yugoslavia, when a census was under way, that in addition to ethnically defining themselves as Muslim, Serbs or Croats, they could all define themselves as Yugoslavs? You do know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What exactly did you mean by "others"?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: There were a number of citizens in Samac, not too many of them though, who were ethnic Albanians, Bulgarians, Macedonians. There were some Roma people too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The ethnic make-up of the town of Samac, was it reflected in the 4th Detachment? Did the 4th Detachment too contain Muslims, Serbs, Croats, Yugoslavs, Roma people, Bulgarians, Macedonians and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And I've spoken about that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Finally, will you please just read out what it says on page 2. Who approved this public announcement, and on whose behalf?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: The detachment command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This is the command of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was written on behalf of the command of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will not be needing this document for the time being. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: While testifying before this Honourable Court, what can you tell us about a gathering of citizens on the 20th of April, 1992, a rally held in the front yard of the Buducnost company in Bosanski Samac? What did you speak about then, and on whose orders were you there? Who ordered you to go to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of April, my commander, Radovan Antic, told me: Get ready. Go to the Buducnost company, to the yard. People have been invited there by the secretariat for National Defence, people, military-aged men, mostly men. Speak to them. Address those people and explain the views of our command, of the members of our 4th Detachment, in connection with this new situation. My estimate was that there were over 200 people assembled there, and I was accompanied by the head of the then ministry, or rather, department, or secretariat for National Defence, Milos Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Among those 200 or more people, what were the ethnicities of the people assembled there?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: That's very difficult for me to say, in terms of percentage, in terms of specific figures, but I do know that very few Croats were there, Muslims were the predominant group at that rally, and then Serbs were there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Continue, please. What did you speak to those people about? What did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: That gathering, I conveyed to those people the views of the command of the 4th Detachment and of all the members of the 4th Detachment. I told them that we were making an enormous effort to try to protect people, citizens, property, companies, and so on. I also told them the following: All of you who are men of military age and fit for military service, please feel free to report to our unit. That I said was an opportunity for us to increase our numerical strength and to try to protect the people from torture, from persecution, from robbery, and so on. At one point I even asked an acquaintance of mine, Fikret, his name was Fikret Seljakovic: Are you sure you don't want to join us? The answer was: I do want to join you. After what you've referred to as a gathering, or rather, a rally, a number of people came along, reported to the unit, a number of people asked to be given work assignments, to work in companies in the town, a number of people asked to go to the Red Cross, to work for civilian protection, those who were not as fit as some others were. And then Milos Bogdanovic told them, he explained to them what the procedure was, that they should report there and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can it just be clarified, before -- as to whether this was something the witness heard, was it actually at that rally that people were coming forward saying we want work assignments or whether it was something he heard afterwards. It's just not clear from what the witness has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: These facts you've just spoken about, did you have personal direct knowledge of this? Did people come to speak to you about this? Were you the speaker at this meeting? And another question: On that occasion, were you addressing all those who were assembled there, regardless of their religion or nationality to join the 4th Detachment, telling them that this was the only way to prevent hostilities from breaking out?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I think I've explained this sufficiently, but I'm prepared to answer all your further questions. People came up to me. They spoke to me. They asked me questions. Someone wanted to speak, and they would ask both me and Milos Bogdanovic: How was the procedure? How do I report to the unit? How do I report to the command? What's the procedure for applying for civilian protection? What do I do to apply to get work -- a work assignment in a company? And then we explained this to those who were asking questions, and the consequence was that a number of those people joined us, our unit. They reported to us and they became members of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: To sum it up, you know this from direct experience, you personally witnessed this and took part in this?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony before this court, can you tell us about what happened after the announcement of the 4th Detachment was published, was broadcast on Radio Bosanski Samac? The members of the command of the 4th Detachment, were they subjected to harassment, to acts of terror, to threats? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: I have no special knowledge of that, but I know that in the eyes of those people who held positions of power, our public announcement was not seen in a very favourable light. I know this from conversations I had with people, the people from the SDS, you know, they're not happy, whose radio is that, something along these lines. I can no longer remember the details, but that's what it was about: Who are you, what are you doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Mr. Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Simo Zaric came to see me at my office. That's came to see us. He stormed into the office, looking very agitated, looking even frightened. His face was white. And he said that a member of the Special Forces, known as Vuk, had put a gun to his face, his forehead - I'm not sure where - verbally abusing him all the while. Simo, you're just a low-down communist. No reason for you to stay alive, is there? I'll see more of you later. He was threatening him. He was verbally abusing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you report about this to the Superior Command, the 17th Tactical Group in Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: It was a rule for us to report on all such occurrences to the Superior Command. I'm not sure about this one. I think Simo probably did report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Commander Radovan Antic after that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell us about it, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC
utterances.text: Radovan Antic told me about what he had gone through. He had been picked up, or rather, nabbed, arrested, by Lugar. We only knew these members of Special Forces by their nicknames. We didn't know their first or last names. Then he beat Radovan. He put him in a car. He was with some other people, but I'm not sure. And then he took him to Obudovac, to a prison, a prison. This was not a prison for -- in the proper sense of the word. It was just a mountain privy, or rather, a toilet, he said. The next day, I believe he was released. He reported to the command. When he was back, he said that under these circumstances, he was no longer prepared to be the commander. And he said that he would report all of this to Commander Stevan Nikolic. He also said that under these circumstances, he no longer wished to remain the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have been informed that I should be concluding my examination-in-chief now, because there seems to be a subject that we have to discuss with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes. I was informed by the registry assistant that there were matters counsel wanted to discuss. Yes, the witness can be led out of the courtroom. We will continue with the testimony tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. What matters, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe I should start first with matters of concern for Mr. Zaric. We were informed yesterday and on Status Conference we discussed certain possibilities to proceed in the afternoon session on the following days, and about some possibilities, like videolink or some other -- find out some other way to keep on with these proceedings in the afternoon hours. I had the opportunity to inform Mr. Zaric, my client, about this possibility during the break today, and also he informed me about some new developments in respect to his medical condition. Mr. Zaric has his surgery rescheduled, and he was just informed this morning about this, and he will have his surgery on April 21st. This is the best term that he could arrange for himself, or rather, doctors could arrange for him. Mr. Zaric still has problems, and they're increasing more and more every day. The only medicine -- the only medical he actually receives are painkillers, that last for a certain period of time, and he cannot take more of these. There is those that he can get during one day and nothing more than that. So Mr. Zaric is very concerned about this possibility that even through videolink, he's not certain that he will be able to follow proceedings. And because of that, he also asked me to address the Trial Chamber and kindly ask for him to address, in just a few words, very briefly, about what is happening with him in these days and what are his capabilities of following the procedure in the next days. And also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. On that matter, the Trial Chamber has asked for a medical report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Then I also -- yes. If Your Honours allowed him to address very briefly for just one minute about his positions in respect of this. This was his position towards his Defence counsels, and he just asked us to address the Trial Chamber, to allow him to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Simo Zaric. You need not stand up if you are not feeling well enough to stand up. You can speak from where you're seated. THE ACCUSED ZARIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is not my aim to exaggerate, but this is the price I'm paying for five years of injustice, me being here now. But my health has deteriorated considerably. I'm sure you will see that in the doctor's report. Currently I'm using one particular drug which helps me to numb my pain and which gets me through the morning session of the trial, but it is not advisable for me to take this drug in the afternoon, for a number of reasons. This is the reason I suffer a lot of pain in the afternoon, and I'm glad to have been told yesterday that I would have my operation on the 21st of April, probably. And I hope that after that, this problem will be resolved. I hope it will not prove a more dangerous problem than I now believe. I have waited for five years for a chance to offer my testimony and for a chance to have my witnesses testifying. So I would just like to ask you for a little extension and to be given the opportunity to defend my own dignity, as well as my own health. It is my health that commands me to speak this way to you now, and I hope that you will be understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, concerning the same problem addressed by Mr. Zaric's Defence, and also on account of the instructions we received today for the further course of this trial, just a couple of words. What I said at the Status Conference the other day, I verified about Miroslav Tadic's 92 bis witnesses, viva voce, those who should be invited. Three of those witnesses already have valid travel documents. Two of them are very busy people, businessmen. They're especially busy next week, as things are. As for other two witnesses, we've started the procedure. We've applied for their travel documents and we have personally intervened with some people at the local SUP to expedite the whole procedure. What I can say is that the week beginning on the 31st of March, or the 1st of April, all four of them, and maybe all five of them, rather, could be able to make it. This very much depends on when their visas are issued. They get their visas in Belgrade or Sarajevo. It usually takes about one or two days and then air tickets can be bought. In our experience so far with witnesses, and everything surrounding their arrival, I think we could make sure that those witnesses are present during the week beginning on the 31st of March. I would like to know the court's decision regarding Mr. Tubakovic and Stojan Damjanovic too, so that we can do the whole package, in a manner of speaking. It's really very difficult for us to come to these witnesses and tell them: You have to be here in two or three days or four days. All these people are very busy. They have their own duties and obligations. They need sometime to organise this. This is after all quite a distance to travel. Secondly, as concerns the possibility of videolink, my client was in collision to me when I was questioning him here. Miroslav Tadic told me this morning that he did not wish to have videolink. He insisted on sitting in the courtroom even if it goes on for the whole day. I told him that his doctor would not exactly recommend that, but he insisted on actually being present in the courtroom. He does not wish to be isolated. He thinks that communication might deteriorate due to that. Regardless of how long the sitting goes on for, he wants to be in the courtroom. He wants to be here. Another thing I would like to say about our defence is: When our witnesses are here, I would please ask for the trial to be organised in such a way that we're not separated from Mr. Tadic in the morning or in the afternoon respectively. The Defence believes this is very essential, for a simple reason: When we go on for the whole day, the one and a half hour lunch break can only be used for our contact, for us to talk to our client. If our client is taken away back to detention after the morning session, then we have a situation where we're no longer able to communicate with our client, because no visits are possible after 5.00 in the afternoon. So we're separated for the duration of those days, which means that we cannot prepare testimonies. So as far as our witnesses are concerned, we think it's necessary for the trial to be organised, or if his health is good enough, to be present for the whole time, then it will not be a problem for us to work with him during the one and a half hour break. But if he's taken back to detention and we have no communication with him, then for us this poses a serious professional problem indeed, and my client also appealed to be allowed -- to apply to be allowed to address the Trial Chamber. I think he has sufficiently demonstrated his desire to go on with this trial, even when he was feeling ill, and again, he's adamant about this, and it is in my professional interest to ensure that he gets a proper defence, so these are in collision. So if you would just allow Mr. Tadic to say a couple of words and to express his own views concerning this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Miroslav Tadic. THE ACCUSED TADIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Lukic has made my views seem a bit more mild than it actually is. But I said that I would be here at all costs. I will not enumerate all my ailments. I will try and do my best to endure, but I'm not sure I can make it. Last time when I was testifying, when I said that I put everything in my life in the service of this trial, I wanted to use one last sentence and to say that I want some -- I want a part of me to sort of remain once this trial is over. With sessions going on as up to this point, which means either the morning session or the afternoon session, I think it would be much easier for Mr. Zaric and for myself to endure, and this would give us a chance to preserve some of our health at least once this trial is over. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Any other counsel? We'll adjourn and continue our proceedings tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 20th day of March 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
